blocks.text: It makes trees waste away and renders the grass withered. And Damir: لعابه سم ناقع النبات والشجر لا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه [luʿābuhu samm nāqiʿ al-nabāt wa-l-shajar lā yaqaʿu ʿalā shayʾ minhu illā ahlakahu], Its saliva is a most potent poison to plants and trees, so that whatever it falls upon, it destroys. Muffet, following Valeriola, reports the same thing in these words: They harm crops, pastures, meadows, gardens and orchards not only by their bite, but also by their dung, which is black, green, biting and heavy, and above all by their bilious and acrid saliva, which they pour from their mouths in quantity while gnawing.

In verse fifteen: Alas for that day! for the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come as devastation from the Almighty. The day of the Lord, that is, the day on which he will sit as [col. 471] judge to punish the Jews by sending the swarm of locusts against them. For learned men rightly observe that day is taken here for judgment. So in 1 Cor. IV, 3. With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of man's day, that is, by human judgment. Jerome writes to Algasia, in Question 10, that this was how the Cilicians spoke, from whom Paul came. I would believe that they borrowed it from their neighbours the Syrians. As devastation from the Almighty] In Hebrew כשד משדי, an elegant paronomasia, as if someone were to say in Greek ὡς ἀπώλειαν ἀπ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνος [hōs apōleian ap᾽ Apollōnos], or ὡς δήωσιν ἐκ Δηοῦς [hōs dēōsin ek Dēous]. Yet the divine name שדי saddai does not mean devastator, but παντοκράτορα [pantokratora], almighty, just as in Arabic شد [shadda] sadda means to strengthen.

In verse sixteen: Is not the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?] Hence it again appears that the subject is the temple while still standing, [III, 299] not as overthrown by the Chaldeans, as Abarbanel holds. By joy is meant the joy of those who cheerfully ate of the sacrifices and firstfruits offered in God's temple, as the Law commands, Deut. XII, 6. 7. Thither ye shall bring your burnt offerings, and your sacrifices, and your tithes, and the offerings of your hand, etc. That there, eating before the Lord your God, ye may rejoice, ye and your households, etc. And Deut. XVI, 10. 11. Thou shalt keep the feast of weeks unto the Lord thy God with a freewill offering, etc. And thou shalt rejoice before the Lord thy God. And 1 Paralip. XIX, 21. 22. They sacrificed unto the Lord, etc. And they did eat and drink before the Lord on that day with great gladness. So, when Alcinous offers sacrifice to Jupiter, Odyssey book 3, the Phaeacians
Μηρὰ δὲ κήαντες δαίνυντ᾽, ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα Τερπόμενοι· — — — — — [Mēra de kēantes dainynt᾽, erikydea daita Terpomenoi]
Roasting the thighs, they feasted, delighting in a splendid banquet. But this joy ceases when offerings are lacking. And they were lacking, because the locusts had left nothing untouched.
